argentina.note: Constitutional privacy weighs against a general bulk crime database. Identity documentation and police checks coexist with uncertain universal carrying obligations, so the identification claim is conditional. Judicial remedies constrain movement and ordinary searches; peaceful associations do not require discretionary permission. Roadblock restrictions do not establish association licensing.

australia.note: Telecommunications metadata retention supports bulk records collection, distinct from contents. Identification duties apply in specified encounters rather than universal compulsory papers. Court-issued control orders retain challenge rights. Designated weapons-search zones are a genuine suspicionless-search exception outside immediate emergencies. Civic association is generally free despite public-order rules.

bangladesh.note: Retained reporting describes communications controls, security enforcement and intimidation alongside partial post-2024 liberalisation. Those practices favour qualified permission for the four coercive mechanisms and restrictive association administration. Restored court provisions and uneven implementation argue against treating every power as unlimited.

bhutan.note: Constitutional privacy and procedure weigh against unrestricted bulk collection, denial of review and routine suspicionless searches. The citizenship/security-clearance system supplies contextual support for compulsory identity documentation; the exact carrying obligation remains inferred. Civil-society regulation is more permission-dependent than mere informal assembly, although application varies.

brazil.note: Constitutional secrecy of communications and free association constrain broad collection and association permission. Identification for lawful policing is not the same as universal paper carrying, warranting a conditional response. Court remedies oppose unreviewable movement restrictions. Violent and discriminatory search practice conflicts with individual constitutional protections, making the search response substantively mixed.

canada.note: Intelligence collection and allied data sharing coexist with domestic Charter constraints, making bulk records permission conditional rather than an extension of targeted wiretap warrants. There is no general compulsory identity-card carrying rule. Peace bonds involve courts; privacy, arbitrary-detention protection and free association weigh strongly against the other revised permissions.

china.note: Security surveillance, real-name systems, political movement controls and tightly supervised civil organisations support broad state discretion. Identity-card presentation has specified statutory contexts, so the universal carrying-and-request formulation is qualified rather than strongly supported. Formal remedies do not establish prompt independent control of political restrictions in practice.

costa-rica.note: Constitutional communications and personal safeguards oppose blanket bulk collection and unreviewable movement control. Civic association is a right rather than discretionary licensing. National identity-document institutions make identification obligations plausible, with the exact carry-on-request rule inferred. Ordinary searches still require grounds despite legitimate security operations.

cuba.note: Political surveillance, prevention of dissent, constrained remedies and state supervision of associations support the revised broad-control claims. Identity papers and security checks favour agreement, but the precise universal carrying duty is less securely established. Written privacy clauses remain counter-evidence; actual political enforcement governs the interpretation.

denmark.note: Intelligence and long-lived data systems supply qualified support for records collection beyond individual suspects. There is no general national identity-card carrying obligation. Legal review remains available for exclusion measures. Statutory weapons-search zones permit some suspicionless searches outside immediate emergencies. Constitutionally free associations are distinct from assembly restrictions.

egypt.note: Retained implementation reporting describes intrusive communications monitoring, arbitrary detention, weak remedies and severe civil-society restrictions. Those practices strongly support broad control rather than court-supervised permission. Identity documentation is plausible within security policing, but the exact all-adults carrying provision is an educated estimate rather than a retrieved statute.

ethiopia.note: Conflict-related coercion, communications controls and detention concerns weigh towards actual security discretion, with constitutional protections and regional variation qualifying intensity. Identity and civil-organisation requirements are estimated from the retained institutional context, not asserted as fully consolidated current laws. Formal rights do not settle practice.

france.note: Intelligence powers support qualified bulk communications records collection. Police can check identity, but obligatory carrying of a national identity card is a stronger claim. Administrative movement restrictions retain legal challenge. Broader identity-check and security-search powers support qualified suspicionless searches. Peaceful association under the general civil framework is not discretionary prior permission.

germany.note: Foreign intelligence collection supplies qualified bulk-records support while constitutional and judicial limits remain. Having identity documentation differs from a general carrying obligation. Courts constrain preventive police powers. Land-specific exceptions do not establish unrestricted routine personal searches. Free association is distinct from registration of legal entities.

hungary.note: Inherited surveillance and broad security policing support qualified records and identity controls. Judicial rights coexist with concerns about effective independence, making denial of prompt review a genuinely conditional interpretation. Organisational pressure and restrictive public-order practice qualify the constitutional right of association but do not establish a universal licensing requirement.

india.note: Security surveillance, extended detention and restrictions on dissent favour broad records and movement-control powers in practice. Aadhaar and citizenship documentation do not by themselves establish mandatory everyday carrying for all adults. Security searches and restrictive NGO oversight support qualified agreement; constitutional rights and ordinary remedies are counter-evidence.

indonesia.note: National identity-document and communications-control institutions support qualified authority. Current court corrections and retained security restrictions compete on prompt review and ordinary search, producing substantive mixed responses. Regulated civil organisations supply a permission-oriented tendency, but notification and legal-entity registration must not be treated automatically as licensing.

iran.note: UN findings and retained research describe severe digital, moral and security controls and weak effective protection from political coercion. Independent civil organisation faces substantive permission constraints. Identity documentation is a plausible ordinary-control tool but its precise universal carrying rule remains less certain than the documented repression.

israel.note: Extensive security surveillance, identity checks and administrative restrictions favour qualified authority. Civilian judicial protections contrast with occupied-territory enforcement and delayed remedies. Peaceful civic organisation exists within Israel while security restrictions and territory-specific administration constrain it; the association response is mixed across the deliberately retained scope.

italy.note: Security intelligence supports qualified records collection, with constitutional judicial safeguards. Identification duties do not imply a general obligation to carry papers. Preventive measures retain challenge rights. Broad public-order exceptions compete with individual search requirements, producing a conditional search response. Peaceful association is protected without general prior permission.

japan.note: Judicial warrants and constitutional expression/privacy weigh against the revised blanket powers. Strict drugs and firearms policy is not evidence for indiscriminate surveillance or unrestricted police searches. Resident/noncitizen document duties do not establish universal carrying for every adult. Civil associations remain distinct from regulated security investigations.

malaysia.note: Identity-card requirements, security policing, sedition and regulated civil organisation support broader authority. Security detention and weak practical remedies favour agreement on restricted access to prompt review, but legal courts remain meaningful counter-evidence. General association regulation is more than permission to prevent a particular violent gathering.

mexico.note: Surveillance and uneven due process support qualified bulk-records and movement-control discretion. Voter credentials are not a general mandatory carry-and-show identity regime. Constitutional search limits compete with coercive actual policing. Constitutional civic association opposes general prior permission despite intimidation and uneven enforcement.

netherlands.note: Intelligence records powers favour qualified bulk authority. The official identification guidance requires a reason for police requests and permits nonsuspect public-order checks; it is not arbitrary request or unlimited compulsory carrying, so ordinary agreement is more likely than strong agreement. Courts remain available against exclusions; designated weapons searches are a real suspicionless exception. Civic association is generally free.

new-zealand.note: Intelligence and records collection favour qualified bulk authority rather than simple extension of targeted warrants. No general compulsory identity-card regime applies to all adults. Control orders retain review, and urgent warrantless entry is an emergency exception expressly excluded from the revised ordinary-search claim. Gang restrictions do not establish universal peaceful-association licensing.

nigeria.note: Communications controls, coercive security practice and prolonged detention favour qualified authority, with written rights as counter-evidence. Identity requirements are inferred from security administration, not from a fully retrieved universal carrying law. Civic groups exist and formal registration is not always discretionary permission, while intimidation and administrative restrictions make the association response mixed.

north-korea.note: Retained reporting on device monitoring, compulsory identification, warrantless inspections, movement control and suppression of independent organisation supports strong permission for each revised mechanism. This evidence concerns actual control rather than assuming that all unrelated health or traffic powers follow from the regime label.

norway.note: Intelligence and communications-records systems supply qualified bulk support, with safeguards. National identity documentation is not universal mandatory carrying. Review of preventive measures and individual-search limits weigh against the broader claims. Free civic association is separate from public safety and permitted road checks.

pakistan.note: Security surveillance, prolonged detention and assembly/content restrictions support qualified broad authority. Identity institutions and civil-organisation oversight favour permission-oriented estimates, while constitutional rights and judicial procedures qualify every inference. Mandatory registration alone is not proof of a discretionary licence for every informal group.

philippines.note: Security operations and intimidation support qualified broad records collection and coercive preventive practice. A national identification system coexists with protections against treating lack of a card as automatic grounds for deprivation, making compulsory carrying mixed. Violent policing qualifies written search protections. Civil association remains generally available despite harassment and red-tagging.

poland.note: Security institutions supply qualified records-collection support within privacy constraints. Required possession of identity documentation is not equivalent to compulsory everyday carrying. Procedural rights and individual search grounds oppose the expanded permissions. Association is constitutionally protected, while reporting and legal registration are narrower obligations.

russia.note: Intrusive communications rules, criminalisation of dissent, preventive security restrictions and weak remedies strongly support broad state control in practice. Identity checks favour ordinary agreement while a universal carrying rule remains less directly established. Civil organisations face substantive approval and closure controls, beyond routine registration.

saudi-arabia.note: Digital monitoring, restrictions on dissent and severe civil-organisation limits support broad authority. Security detention limits prompt independent recourse. Identity-document and search controls favour qualified agreement, acknowledging formal procedures and licensed activities rather than assuming every power is unbounded.

singapore.note: Communications/security powers support bulk-records collection subject to operational limits. Identity-document duties favour qualified permission without a freshly consolidated all-adults carrying rule. Preventive security detention and restrictive societies administration strongly support the review/association claims. Recent warrantless powers qualify the ordinary-search safeguards.

south-africa.note: Surveillance and statutory interception coexist with privacy jurisprudence, producing a conditional bulk-records judgement. Universal carrying is not established by identity-document possession. The Bill of Rights protects independent remedies and association. Area-authorised security searches remain a qualified suspicionless exception despite constitutional reasonableness requirements.

south-korea.note: Judicial interception procedures and constitutional anonymity/privacy protections favour individual rather than generalised grounds. Identity systems do not automatically require carrying for every ordinary encounter. Court-backed preventive measures are not denial of review. Police questioning/search grounds and free association weigh against the broader revised permissions.

spain.note: Security intelligence and broad public-order identity checks favour qualified records and identification powers, with document possession/carrying differences disclosed. Preventive measures retain legal challenge. Public-security search exceptions support qualified suspicionless authority. Peaceful associations require notification/registration in some forms rather than general discretionary permission.

sweden.note: Intelligence interception and communications records collection favour qualified bulk authority. No general compulsory identity-card carrying regime applies. Preventive exclusions retain judicial review. Security zones expressly allow suspicionless searches outside immediate emergencies. Constitutionally protected association is distinct from conditions imposed on gatherings.

switzerland.note: Intelligence and communications-records powers supply qualified broad collection. National documents are not a universal carrying requirement. Preventive terrorism measures remain contestable. Cantonal preventive policing and concrete-danger thresholds compete on searches outside emergencies, producing a conditional rather than unrestricted answer. Peaceful associations generally form freely.

taiwan.note: Communications warrants require evidence and necessity. Identity checks at risk locations are not a general compulsory-carry rule, and intrusive searches require additional grounds. Newly court-supervised psychiatric detention exemplifies review rather than its denial. Constitutional assembly and civic organisation protections oppose discretionary association permission.

thailand.note: Security and speech restrictions support qualified communications, identity and preventive discretion. Courts and ordinary rights remain counter-evidence to unrestricted control. Civic organisations function alongside administrative regulation and repression; legal registration is not uniformly discretionary permission, making that question genuinely mixed.

turkey.note: Political speech prosecutions, security restrictions and assembly controls favour broad actual enforcement, with formal judicial rights qualifying intensity. Identity and association requirements are interpreted contextually rather than asserted as complete statutory consolidation. Effective remedies, not the existence of a court label alone, govern the movement-control estimate.

ukraine.note: Wartime checkpoints, movement restrictions and security operations favour qualified authority; they do not imply an unconditional peacetime regime. Courts and protest space coexist with delayed or exceptional wartime recourse, making prompt review mixed. Civil organisations remain active, so war controls do not establish general licensing of peaceful association.

united-arab-emirates.note: Extensive actual surveillance, constrained political expression and restrictive civil organisation strongly support bulk and association controls. Security detention weakens prompt independent remedies. Identification and searches favour qualified authority; exact universal carrying/search provisions remain contextual estimates, not fully retrieved statutory findings.

united-kingdom.note: Investigatory Powers Act bulk acquisition is a real broad-records power with warrants and oversight, not a mere targeted wiretap. Ordinary encounters do not require universal identity papers. Preventive orders retain legal challenge. Authorised area searches remain a real suspicionless exception outside immediate emergencies. Peaceful civic association is not universally licensed.

united-states.note: Intelligence records collection and incidental acquisition favour qualified bulk permission, tempered by reforms ending particular domestic bulk programmes. Hiibel permits compelled identity during a justified stop, not compulsory universal paper carrying. Judicial review conflicts with executive practices seeking rapid removals, making effective prompt review mixed. Wardlow/Edmond require individual grounds outside narrow emergency exceptions; peaceful association is protected.

vietnam.note: Surveillance, political house arrest and strong restrictions on independent organisation support broad authority in practice. Identity and security searches favour qualified permission, acknowledging incomplete consolidation of their precise general thresholds. Formal courts do not establish prompt independent recourse for political movement restrictions.

alt-lite.note: The retained school combines anti-censorship claims with law-and-order support. Broad surveillance, identification and searches therefore involve substantive conflicting commitments, rather than automatic liberty from its label. Judicial challenge and voluntary peaceful organisation fit better than denial of remedies or general licensing.

american-conservatism.note: Constitutional speech, arms and private life constrain arbitrary control. Strong policing does not establish bulk records, compulsory papers or searches lacking grounds. Independent review and voluntary civic institutions fit the retained constitutional strand especially strongly. Security-oriented conservatives remain counter-evidence to treating the tradition as uniformly libertarian.

anarcho-capitalism.note: Self-ownership and voluntary protection oppose state bulk collection, compulsory documents, unreviewable restrictions and suspicionless searches. Peaceful association requires consent of participants rather than state permission. Private property and responses to actual aggression qualify other retained questions; opposition to state police is not support for violence.

authoritarian-capitalism.note: The retained institutional model prioritises security monitoring and managed civil organisation alongside economic predictability. Identity and coercive policing are supported with practical legal qualifications. Independent remedies can exist, but public-order discretion is more central than a guaranteed prompt challenge against each restriction.

christian-accelerationism.note: The specified national-power/technology variant combines entrepreneurial privacy with strong security and moral order. Its records-collection and civic-control tendency is not imported from every Christian or technological movement. Compulsory papers, denial of review and routine searches have real tension with the retained escape-from-coercion strand, supporting conditional answers.

christian-conservatism.note: Personal and religious liberties, constitutional procedure and voluntary congregational life oppose the expanded permissions. Moral restraints and order qualify the strength of that opposition, especially for associations seen as conflicting with public morality. Religious conviction alone is not evidence of support for surveillance.

christian-democracy.note: Human dignity, subsidiarity and autonomous civic institutions favour independent remedies and free association. Targeted lawful crime prevention does not establish bulk or suspicionless powers. Identification has competing practical public-administration and personal-autonomy considerations, so this is a conditional judgement rather than missing-evidence neutrality.

christian-social-democracy.note: Dignity and social responsibility support ordinary safety measures while preserving privacy, effective legal recourse and peaceful civic organisation. The revised denial of safeguards is therefore less compatible than the old court-supervised measures. Solidarity does not imply indiscriminate state intrusion.

christian-socialism.note: The retained communitarian freedom and voluntary organising support private life and effective remedies. Collective responsibility can justify proportionate prevention of harm, but not automatic bulk collection, universal compulsory papers or permission to form every peaceful association.

civic-nationalism.note: Common civic membership and rights support independent review and voluntary organisations. Legitimate public-order institutions are retained but do not settle the much broader revised police powers. National identity as civic membership is not a requirement to carry state identity papers.

classical-liberalism.note: The harm principle and individual rights oppose intrusive control without individual grounds. Court-supervised action against actual threats remains compatible with the doctrine; denial of review and general association permission are different mechanisms. Strong opposition follows the literal rights claims, not confidence about a historical modern questionnaire.

communism.note: The retained party-state school uses security supervision and controlled organising, not an assumed identical position for every communist thinker. Formal procedures qualify compulsory identification and ordinary searches, but do not establish prompt independent constraint of political restrictions or unlicensed civic competition.

communitarianism.note: The responsive communal model explicitly combines common-good responsibilities with protection from arbitrary detention and privacy violations. Safety and administrative identity duties compete with autonomy on the first two claims. Effective review is strongly favoured; routine suspicionless searches and discretionary association licensing go beyond proportionate obligations.

conservative-centrism.note: The retained One Nation/ECHR scope combines public safety and accepted intelligence powers with privacy and fair-trial protections. Bulk records are conditional under that tension. The rights framework rejects denial of review and licensing peaceful civic organisations, while general compulsory papers and suspicionless searches receive weaker support than targeted policing.

constitutional-monarchism.note: The constitutional variant constrains the state through independent courts and civic rights. A monarch as an institutional form does not determine support for surveillance or papers. Lawful policing remains possible; unreviewable restrictions and prior permission for peaceful association conflict with the selected rights-based scope.

cuban-socialism.note: The specific Cuban party-state model uses political security, surveillance and supervised associations. Written civil rights remain counter-evidence, especially on the precise scope of identity and ordinary search powers, but actual dissent and movement controls are not equivalent to independent remedies.

cultural-nationalism.note: The retained cultural-development tradition values expression and associational self-development. Communal identity can impose social obligations without requiring blanket state surveillance, compulsory papers or permission for civic groups. The modern police scenarios remain explicit historical inferences.

democratic-socialism.note: The specified democratic/abolitionist programme protects organising, bodily autonomy and resistance to intrusive policing. It supports remedies against state restrictions rather than an unreviewable security discretion. Public provision and redistribution are not evidence for these coercive permissions.

ecosocialism.note: Democratic transformation and collective organisation require civil liberties and effective legal recourse. Ecological harm prevention is not a warrant for mass communications collection or arbitrary personal searches. Opposition is qualified where exact modern identity and intelligence practice is not specified, without converting uncertainty into centrism.

environmentalism.note: The retained environmental information/protest framework protects public organising and participation. Harm-prevention policy can be coercive but differs from suspicionless police intrusion and denial of challenge. Environmental regulation does not establish licensing every peaceful civic association.

fascism.note: The specified doctrine subordinates dissent and voluntary organising to state discipline. Political police and executive authority support broad monitoring, searches and restrictions without independent challenge. The precise all-adults documentation mechanism is inferred with ordinary rather than strong agreement.

green-politics.note: The retained universal-rights and participatory programme protects privacy, peaceful organising and safeguards against arbitrary coercion. Legitimate prevention of violence is separate from intrusion without individual grounds. Strong rights commitments support strong opposition on the relevant mechanisms even when modern policy details remain inferred.

hindu-nationalism.note: The selected national-security/social-discipline programme supports broader security administration while retaining civil institutions and justice language. Each exact mechanism is a qualified inference rather than a movement-wide documented answer. Private Hindu belief alone provides no evidence for these responses.

islamic-fundamentalism.note: The specified Qutb-derived scope combines moral/security discipline with liberation from arbitrary human domination. Identification is conditional because civic administration and opposition to personal tyranny compete. The other mechanisms favour qualified control, with exact legal safeguards and peaceful-association limits unsettled; this is not a position assigned to all Muslims.

islamic-socialism.note: The specified historical mobilisation combines popular organisation with executive coercion. Security records and identity administration favour authority. Popular civil activity and formal accountability compete with restrictive practice on review, searches and association, producing genuine mixed answers rather than neutrality from religious identity.

islamism.note: The selected political-religious state model supervises morality, security and organisation. Procedural institutions qualify the first four coercive permissions; peaceful association that challenges the governing order is not simply free of substantive state permission. This scope is distinct from religious belief or every Islamic movement.

kantian-republicanism.note: Public reason and rightful general law reject arbitrary restriction and searches without grounds. Legal coercion may protect equal freedom, but it is not sufficient evidence for bulk monitoring or compulsory papers. Public order and historical limits on civic activity qualify the exact association answer.

left-wing-populism.note: The retained pluralist mobilisation uses criticism, protest and independent civic organisation against elite power. Harm prevention can justify targeted safeguards; the revised broader control claims have weaker fit. The populist label does not itself establish either unchecked executive power or absolute libertarianism.

liberal-conservatism.note: Individual freedoms coexist with lawful order, with independent courts qualifying enforcement. Targeted policing does not imply mass communications collection, universal compulsory papers or searches lacking grounds. Civil society and legal remedies strongly oppose the expanded review/association claims.

liberal-feminism.note: Bodily autonomy, equal liberties and freedom from domination protect privacy and voluntary organising. Protection from violence can justify individual action under safeguards; it does not establish intrusive unchecked powers over nonsuspects. Identity documentation remains a qualified modern application rather than a claim about every feminist programme.

liberalism.note: The retained manifesto and rights framework protect expression, privacy and association. Proportionate crime prevention remains legitimate with individual grounds and remedies. Strong opposition to unreviewable control follows the doctrine while the precise compulsory-paper scenario remains a qualified application.

libertarianism.note: The retained self-ownership/privacy platform opposes indiscriminate surveillance and coercion, compulsory identification, and unchecked police powers. Voluntary association does not need state permission. Property rights and responding to actual violence remain distinct from these blanket permissions.

luxemburgism.note: Public dissent, political discussion and self-emancipation oppose security bureaucracy and licensing political/civic organisation. Revolutionary defence against actual violence creates qualifications for precise search/identity mechanisms, but is not a reason to permit arbitrary restrictions without challenge.

maoism.note: The specified revolutionary-control model distinguishes enemies from the participating people and permits coercive suppression. Security monitoring and managed associations are strongly compatible. Formal participation within the revolutionary camp does not create independent review for those restricted; universal identity carrying remains a qualified modern analogy.

marxism.note: The retained emancipatory theory opposes censorship, political policing and barriers to workers organising. Transitional coercion against actual oppression qualifies the scope of opposition, but is not imported from later party-states as a general surveillance doctrine. Peaceful collective association is particularly central.

meritocracy.note: The selected opportunity/inquiry model benefits from independent safeguards and freedom to organise, not unchecked coercion. Fair administration may support identity verification while privacy opposes general compulsory carrying, producing a substantive conditional answer. Expertise does not itself determine a police-control position.

militarism.note: Security and secrecy support records collection and stronger policing in the retained civilian-institutional scope. Independent civilian checks compete with security urgency on review and association, making those claims mixed. Military strength alone is not evidence for abolishing every civilian liberty.

minarchism.note: The minimal protective state can act against actual rights violations through objective judicial procedures. That does not extend to blanket records collection, compulsory papers, suspicionless searches, unreviewable restrictions or permission to form peaceful groups. These modern applications follow the specific rights principle.

nationalist-conservatism.note: National order and family duties coexist with constitutional rights in the retained scope. Security and privacy compete over bulk records, papers and routine searches. Independent recourse and autonomous civic organisation have more support than denial/licensing, qualified by the programme’s public-order priorities.

nazism.note: Political policing, identification and racial regulation, detention without effective independent remedy and suppression of autonomous organisations directly support broad control in this historical scope. Selective permission for favoured groups is not universal civic freedom.

neoconservatism.note: Counterterrorism intelligence receives substantial weight while constitutional speech and judicial safeguards remain central. Security exceptions and legal restraints genuinely compete on prompt review and searches. Support for force abroad is not sufficient evidence for universal domestic papers or licensing peaceful associations.

neoliberalism.note: Private choice and predictable general law oppose arbitrary police interference. Targeted judicial action against harms remains compatible, but denial of review and general association permission are different propositions. Economic market policy does not supply the answers; the retained individual-rights context does.

nordic-social-democracy.note: The retained Nordic institutional model combines privacy/civic rights with intelligence and preventive public-order measures. These competing commitments make broad records and suspicionless searches conditional. Effective legal recourse and free peaceful association remain stronger than security discretion; universal papers are not implied by welfare administration.

objectivism.note: Objective individual rights and law against initiated force oppose the revised blanket coercive claims. Protection against actual force must have a rights-based legal justification. Peaceful civic association requires voluntary consent, with no general state permission even where a minimal government remains.

postmodernism.note: The specified critical theory of discipline, surveillance and normalisation strongly opposes these permissions as instruments of arbitrary control. This is an explicitly inferred application of the selected anti-domination strand, not a claim that all postmodern authors have one complete police platform.

progressive-liberalism.note: The retained Deweyan scope values public inquiry, association and personal rights while accepting public responsibility. Protection from harms can justify bounded intervention; the revised lack of grounds or review goes beyond it. Modern identification and bulk collection remain contextual applications.

republicanism.note: Freedom as non-domination particularly opposes unchallengeable discretion and interference without justified grounds. Non-arbitrary lawful protection remains permissible, so targeted prevention is not rejected automatically. Independent peaceful civic organising is incompatible with general permission from the power it may criticise.

right-wing-populism.note: The retained Reform/law-and-order scope mixes anti-censorship and freedom claims with stronger police proposals. Records and identity powers involve competing commitments. Expanded policing supports searches more than denial of independent recourse; organisation remains generally free but public-order priorities qualify opposition to licensing.

social-anarchism.note: Opposition to state hierarchy and coercive domination rejects surveillance, compulsory papers, unreviewable restrictions, suspicionless searches and licensing peaceful groups. Collective self-defence against actual violence is distinct from conferring those general police powers.

social-democracy.note: The retained international declaration protects expression, association and freedom from arbitrary detention. Public safety and welfare responsibilities permit proportionate legal measures, not general intrusion without safeguards. The revised review and association claims therefore draw strong opposition.

social-liberalism.note: Effective individual freedom and preventing harm coexist under general legal constraints. Public provision does not establish compulsory papers or surveillance of nonsuspects. Independent recourse and autonomous association are strong liberal commitments; precise modern policing applications remain qualified.

socialism.note: The retained broad democratic/anti-domination scope requires the ability to organise and resist arbitrary power. Solidarity can support proportionate health and safety rules but does not justify unreviewable restriction or general association permission. Later authoritarian governments are not substituted for this assessed school.

thatcherism.note: Law and order and counterterrorism coexist with civil constitutional protections in the specified historical scope. Targeted interception and executive security discretion create a conditional bulk-records/review interpretation rather than assuming later intelligence practice. Broad counterterrorism search powers support qualified authority. Civic organisations generally exist despite restraints on coercive industrial action.

third-way.note: The retained active-public-safety model accepts stronger intelligence and administrative intervention while retaining civil inclusion and legal safeguards. Identity and search duties compete with privacy and proportionality. Legal review and peaceful civic organisation are not abandoned by the programme’s crime-prevention commitments.

traditional-conservatism.note: Ordered liberty and established legal procedure oppose arbitrary power while preserving public peace and moral obligations. Targeted lawful measures are compatible; the revised blanket claims have weaker fit. Historical limits on associations and the broad school’s variations qualify response strength without treating all conservatives alike.

trotskyism.note: Workers’ mobilisation and anti-bureaucratic scrutiny require civic speech and organising. Coercion against armed counter-revolution qualifies the specific security mechanisms, but is not permission to license all peaceful organisations or remove every remedy. The retained school is not inferred from Stalinist practice.

zionism.note: The retained lawful civic/national-security design combines individual rights with security discretion. Records, identification and searches therefore remain conditional modern applications. Judicial recourse and civic organisation have more support than arbitrary denial/licensing. Neither private Jewish identity nor a current government is substituted for the specified historical doctrine.

abraham-lincoln.note: Wartime habeas suspension and restrictions on dissent support security discretion beyond ordinary warrants. Compulsory identity papers and licensing every peaceful civic group are conditional: mobilisation and executive urgency compete with constitutional civilian life. Modern bulk records are an explicit analogy to security intelligence, not a claim about digital policy.

adam-smith.note: Natural liberty and criticism of arbitrary power weigh against blanket intrusion. Ordinary justice and historical legal restrictions qualify the strength of opposition. Modern records and papers are inferred applications of personal security, not answers imported from his market policy.

adolf-hitler.note: Political policing, racial identification, detention without meaningful independent remedy and suppression of autonomous organisations strongly support the revised controls. Modern bulk communications records are a disclosed technological analogy to the documented security state.

alexandria-ocasio-cortez.note: Her Ban Flock/privacy and immigrant-rights record opposes mass tracking and intrusive police power. Independent recourse and peaceful organising are central. Exact compulsory paper carrying remains a qualified inference, not derived from opposition to every form of identity verification.

andy-burnham.note: The Hillsborough accountability campaign strongly favours meaningful independent remedies. Public-protection duties coexist with concern about institutional abuse, making bulk records conditional. Suspicionless ordinary searches and papers have weaker support than targeted enforcement; peaceful civic association is not general licensing.

angela-merkel.note: Security intelligence coexists with proportionality and constitutional remedies in the assessed chancellorship. German identity possession is not universal carrying. Area/security exceptions qualify the search claim but do not imply searches in every routine encounter. Civic organisations remain generally autonomous.

angus-taylor.note: Individual choice/speech and stronger intelligence screening coexist. Screening noncitizens and compulsory visa social-media disclosure do not establish bulk collection of everyone’s records or universal identity papers. Legal review and peaceful domestic organisations remain more compatible with his retained programme than the expanded coercive claims.

anthony-albanese.note: Security/data retention and harm regulation support qualified records authority, with courts and civil expression retained. Identification is not universal carrying. Federal and state public-order exceptions compete with individual search rights, making searches conditional. Gun or digital-harm regulation does not establish licensing peaceful civic association.

augusto-pinochet.note: Secret police, political detention and censorship support strong control over surveillance, review, searches and autonomous organisation. Exact universal identity-paper carrying is a qualified inference rather than a separately retrieved personal position. Economic privatisation does not supply these answers.

ayn-rand.note: Individual rights and objective laws against initiated force strongly oppose blanket coercive permissions. A protective government may prosecute actual rights violations but does not license peaceful association or remove judicial safeguards. Modern records/papers remain explicitly inferred applications of her rights theory.

barack-obama.note: His administration retained extensive intelligence collection while reforming the domestic bulk telephony programme. Judicial commitments coexist with counterterrorism detention and remedies disputes, so prompt review is mixed rather than wholly rejected. Ordinary papers/searches and peaceful associations do not follow automatically from security policy.

benito-mussolini.note: Fascist police coercion, confinement of opponents and suppression of independent organising support the expanded controls. Universal compulsory identity carrying is a qualified historical inference. State doctrine and conduct, rather than a right-wing label, supply the evidence.

benjamin-netanyahu.note: Security detention, communications control and judicial-overhaul conflicts favour broad authority. Meaningful civilian courts and domestic civic organisation coexist with harsher occupied-territory controls, producing a mixed association answer under the retained broad period/scope. Security powers are not portrayed as unlimited in every jurisdiction.

bernie-sanders.note: Privacy criticism, opposition to intrusive tracking and due-process commitments support strong opposition to records collection and unreviewable restriction. Proportionate public protection remains possible. Precise papers/search scenarios are qualified inferences, not derived from his redistribution or economic programme.

bill-gates.note: Responsible public institutions and civil freedoms favour safeguards over arbitrary intrusion. Administrative identification and privacy compete, making compulsory papers conditional. Support for public-health intervention is not evidence for denial of court review or licensing every peaceful group. Exact policing views remain contextual estimates.

bob-hawke.note: Civil institutions and security enforcement coexist in the retained premiership. Bulk communications are a conditional historical extension, not an asserted digital programme. Regulated drugs and health policy do not establish universal papers, unreviewable movement controls or unrestricted searches. Voluntary civic organisation is strongly compatible.

boris-johnson.note: Intelligence and stronger public-order policing favour qualified broad collection and search exceptions. Pandemic and preventive restrictions retained avenues of challenge. Liberty rhetoric and lack of universal identity carrying oppose compulsory papers; ordinary civic associations were not subject to blanket discretionary licensing.

charles-de-gaulle.note: War/unrest security powers favour broad surveillance and policing. Constitutional restoration and civil legal institutions compete with exceptional coercion on prompt review. National identity administration is a qualified historical inference. Civic organisation was constrained in some security cases but not universally licensed.

clement-attlee.note: Emergency powers, wartime/postwar administration and interventions in strikes coexist with parliamentary criticism and civil institutions. The identification, review and search claims are conditional across that scope. Modern bulk records are inferred from security administration. Peaceful groups are not equivalent to strikes judged disruptive.

deng-xiaoping.note: Party security and suppression of dissent support strong broad-control interpretations. Market reform does not establish personal liberty. The universal identification-carrying mechanism is a qualified historical application; formal legal institutions do not imply independent remedies against political restrictions.

donald-trump.note: Retained FISA, tracking, civil-commitment and rapid-removal evidence supports qualified security intrusion and weakened prompt recourse. Constitutional speech and association commitments coexist with scrutiny of NGOs and political organisations; a universal licence for every peaceful group is not established, so association is mixed. Immigration identity checks likewise do not establish mandatory papers for every adult citizen.

dwight-d-eisenhower.note: Cold War intelligence and loyalty screening favour qualified security records as a modern analogy. Constitutional freedoms oppose general denial of remedies or groundless ordinary searches. Identity administration is conditional in that historical context. Restrictions on suspected subversion qualify otherwise free civic organisation.

edmund-burke.note: Ordered liberty and established law oppose arbitrary power while preserving civil peace and moral restraint. The revised blanket permissions have weaker support than legitimate justice. Historical associations and emergency obligations qualify intensity; modern surveillance/papers are explicit analogies, not market-policy deductions.

elon-musk.note: Expression and voluntary personal choices favour resistance to blanket intrusion. Security and criticisms of judicial constraint compete with personal autonomy on prompt review, yielding a mixed response. Investment or technological capability alone is not proof that he supports indiscriminate data collection or association licensing.

emmanuel-macron.note: Security legislation and protest policing favour qualified intelligence and suspicionless exceptions. Courts remain available against restrictions, and identity checks do not create universal carrying. Pressure on some associations qualifies the general freedom of civic organisation without establishing blanket prior licensing.

fidel-castro.note: Political detention, security monitoring and state control of independent organising favour strong authority. Universal identity carrying is a qualified inference. Formal rights and regulated lawful activities remain counter-evidence but do not establish prompt independent remedies against political restrictions.

franklin-d-roosevelt.note: Wartime internment and security administration conflict with civil-liberty commitments. Those actions favour preventive restrictions lacking prompt remedy, while identity papers, ordinary searches and association permission remain mixed across peacetime and wartime practice. Modern bulk records are explicitly a historical analogy.

frederick-douglass.note: Resistance to slavery and arbitrary coercion, free speech and equal legal protection strongly oppose compulsory status papers, unchecked restrictions and barriers to peaceful organising. Modern surveillance is inferred from these personal-security principles, not falsely attributed as a technological statement.

friedrich-hayek.note: Predictable general law and a protected private sphere oppose arbitrary coercion. Harm prevention can justify properly grounded legal action; general bulk collection and unreviewable restrictions go beyond it. Exact compulsory identity documentation is a qualified modern inference rather than economic-score borrowing.

george-w-bush.note: PATRIOT-era collection and warrantless intelligence strongly favour bulk records. Preventive detention conflicts with meaningful recourse, while courts and formal safeguards remain counter-evidence. Identity and ordinary-search duties are mixed across security exceptions and constitutional practice. Peaceful association was generally possible despite counterterrorism scrutiny.

george-washington.note: Lawful order and constitutional personal security favour constraints on ordinary coercion. Historical intelligence and executive enforcement compete with private life on the modern bulk-records analogy. The exact papers/search/association mechanisms remain qualified rather than treating the founding period as unrestricted modern civil libertarianism.

gough-whitlam.note: Civil protections, legal aid and opposition to harsh coercion favour meaningful remedies and voluntary organising. Ordinary criminal enforcement remains possible. Modern records and compulsory-paper scenarios are inferred from the retained civil-rights direction, not attributed as exact contemporary statements.

harry-s-truman.note: Loyalty screening and national intelligence favour qualified broad collection. Vetoes of restrictive anti-subversion measures are counter-evidence to unrestricted control. Compulsory papers and ordinary searches are genuinely mixed with security practice; independent remedies and generally free civic organisation remain more likely than wholesale denial/licensing.

hillary-clinton.note: Intelligence and counterterrorism support favour qualified records authority. Her retained civil-rights and judicial commitments weigh against universal papers, unreviewable movement restrictions and searches without grounds. Peaceful civic association remains strongly protected; exact response intensity is inferred.

ho-chi-minh.note: Party discipline and wartime security favour broad monitoring, movement restriction and supervised organisation. National-liberation commitments do not establish personal protections against the governing party. Identity carrying and ordinary searches are qualified historical inferences rather than a complete retrieved security code.

hugo-chavez.note: Reprisals, media restrictions and weakened courts favour qualified executive control over the new mechanisms. Civic and electoral activity persisted, so strong universal repression is not inferred for every item. Identity and precise bulk-records practices remain contextual estimates under the specified presidency.

indira-gandhi.note: Emergency censorship, preventive detention and coercive population policy strongly support denial of prompt remedies in that period. Modern communications records and police search powers favour qualified authority. A general compulsory-paper regime is mixed with ordinary constitutional life; civic organisation suffered restrictions without every group being permanently licensed.

jacinda-ardern.note: Security institutions and intelligence remain compatible with her programme, while civil criticism and court remedies persist. Pandemic restrictions and gun control do not establish compulsory identity papers, ordinary searches lacking grounds or general licensing of peaceful civic groups.

javier-milei.note: His personal-liberty and voluntary-action commitments oppose blanket state intrusion and permission for civic organising. Strict controls on obstructive protests are counter-evidence on assembly, preserved in its separate question; they do not automatically establish denial of court review or unrestricted ordinary searches.

jawaharlal-nehru.note: Preventive detention and speech restrictions favour qualified security authority despite constitutional liberties. Independent review was not uniformly prompt in security cases. Ordinary identity/search duties retain competing protections, while peaceful organisations generally operated subject to public-order restrictions.

jd-vance.note: Anti-censorship/gun-rights commitments coexist with border enforcement and criticism of judges constraining executive power. Bulk intelligence and prompt review are substantive mixed cases. No recorded vote on the 2024 warrant amendment is treated as a vote for either side. Identity checks and stronger enforcement do not establish universal papers or general groundless searches.

jean-jacques-rousseau.note: Common civic obligations and the sovereign civic order support identity and organisation supervision as historical analogies. The connection between self-government and liberty competes with public discipline on surveillance, remedies and searches. These are genuinely conditional modern applications, not neutral substitutes for missing quotations.

jeff-bezos.note: The retained explicit personal-liberty commitment favours privacy and independent civic organisation. Legitimate intervention against crime was tied to warrants and credible threats, which do not establish the revised blanket permissions. Precise modern police positions remain contextual assumptions.

jeremy-corbyn.note: Opposition to surveillance and intrusive policing, peaceful protest and civil liberties strongly favour safeguards and voluntary organising. Papers remain a qualified specific inference. National economic planning is not used as evidence for state intrusion into personal life.

jimmy-carter.note: Civil liberties and legal accountability weigh against blanket intrusion and unreviewable restriction. Safety regulation is retained separately. Later criticisms of detention/surveillance are contextual rather than silently substituted for the presidency’s exact policy; the revised answers remain inferred.

joe-biden.note: Security intelligence and public protection favour qualified records authority, with constitutional privacy and legal remedies. Gun regulation and public-health measures do not imply compulsory identity papers or permission to form peaceful civic groups. Search exceptions are distinguished from the revised general claim.

joh-bjelke-petersen.note: The retained period’s protest suppression, police power and moral regulation favour broad control. Precise bulk records and identity duties are historical estimates, not independently retrieved universal rules. Civil institutions and ordinary lawful organisations qualify intensity rather than supporting blanket freedom or total repression.

john-f-kennedy.note: Security surveillance and civil-rights enforcement coexist. Court remedies and no universal compulsory-paper commitment oppose broader permissions. Security exceptions and actual surveillance make ordinary police intrusion conditional; civic organisation is generally protected with anti-subversion qualifications.

john-howard.note: Counterterrorism measures and security intelligence favour qualified broad collection. Australian ordinary identity practice does not establish compulsory papers for everyone. Extended preventive restrictions and constitutional safeguards compete on prompt review and searches. Gun controls are not evidence of licensing peaceful civic organisations.

john-locke.note: Standing laws, personal security and life/liberty/property restrain arbitrary coercion. Preservation obligations and legitimate magistrate action qualify opposition, while denial of independent recourse fits particularly poorly. Modern police questions are historical analogies; his exclusions and limited toleration qualify association rather than being erased.

john-maynard-keynes.note: Personal liberty and reform of moral/sexual restrictions oppose arbitrary policing and state permission for peaceful organising. Public regulation and expert administration remain compatible with safeguards. Economic planning is not used to infer support for intrusive police powers.

john-rawls.note: Equal basic liberties include personal integrity, association and fair legal procedure. Measures necessary to safeguard others’ liberties require justification; blanket surveillance and searches without grounds have weaker fit. The specific identification mechanism remains a qualified modern application.

john-stuart-mill.note: The harm principle opposes intrusion into competent adults’ self-regarding conduct and peaceful association. Action to prevent injury can be justified under objective grounds and review. Modern bulk records and papers are explicit applications, with narrower public-safety permissions retained separately.

joseph-stalin.note: Political terror, compulsory population control, security policing and suppression of autonomous organising strongly support the revised coercive mechanisms. Constitutional texts are counter-evidence in form rather than proof of effective independent protection. Digital bulk records remain a disclosed historical analogy.

julia-gillard.note: Security powers and public protection coexist with civil institutions. Broad records collection favours qualified authority, while ordinary identity practice and review rights oppose universal papers and unchallengeable movement restrictions. Jurisdiction-specific search exceptions produce a conditional estimate, distinct from licensing civic organisation.

justin-trudeau.note: Security intelligence remains accepted alongside cannabis liberalisation and Charter protections. Exceptional public-order intervention competes with legal review on the prompt-remedy claim. No general compulsory-paper regime or unrestricted ordinary search power follows from those exceptions. Peaceful civil organisations remain generally free.

kamala-harris.note: A substantial prosecution/public-safety orientation supports qualified intelligence collection. Civil liberties and bodily autonomy favour judicial recourse and personal search grounds. Strong enforcement does not establish compulsory papers for every adult or general licensing of peaceful civic groups.

karl-marx.note: Criticism of censorship and political policing and the need for workers to organise oppose blanket intrusion. Revolutionary action against oppression qualifies security answers, but later party-state practices are not substituted for his own theory. Free peaceful association is especially central.

keir-starmer.note: Stronger policing, intelligence and public-order commitments favour qualified records/search authority. Rule of law supports independent challenge. Administrative identification priorities compete with personal privacy, making the universal-carry claim conditional. Restrictive treatment of some organisations qualifies otherwise free association.

kim-jong-un.note: The retained actual-control evidence concerns pervasive monitoring, identification, movement restrictions, arbitrary detention and suppression of autonomous organisation. Those facts support each revised mechanism without relying on unrelated economics, faith or a political label. Formal legal wording does not establish independent remedies.

lee-kuan-yew.note: Preventive detention, strong security administration and restrictive civic organisation support authority. Independent prompt challenge fits poorly with the assessed security-detention practice. Exact bulk records, papers and ordinary-search details are qualified historical inferences rather than assumptions that all state powers are limitless.

liz-truss.note: Individual freedom and anti-censorship coexist with conventional British intelligence/security support, making bulk records conditional. Ordinary legal safeguards and voluntary civic activity oppose unreviewable restrictions and licensing. The retained programme does not establish compulsory carrying of identity papers.

lula-da-silva.note: Civil institutions and collective organising oppose arbitrary restriction and prior permission for civic groups. Ordinary security intelligence competes with privacy on bulk records, producing a conditional estimate. Criminal enforcement and public-order policy do not automatically establish universal papers or groundless personal searches.

lyndon-b-johnson.note: Security surveillance and public-order interventions coexist with civil-rights enforcement. This favours qualified broad collection, while review/search claims are mixed across coercive practice and constitutional commitments. Peaceful civic organisation remains generally possible despite scrutiny of activists; no universal identity-carrying commitment is established.

mahatma-gandhi.note: Resistance to coercive registration, civil disobedience and freedom of conscience strongly oppose the revised controls. Personal moral discipline is not permission for state papers, surveillance or licensing peaceful groups. Modern records are a disclosed application of his resistance to arbitrary coercion.

mao-zedong.note: Enemy/people distinctions and revolutionary security discipline support broad control over dissent and organisation. Participation inside the revolutionary camp does not confer independent protection on those restricted. Exact universal identity carrying is a qualified historical mechanism, with modern records an explicit analogy.

marco-rubio.note: Constitutional liberties coexist with strongly supported intelligence capabilities. His earlier vote against a warrant-access safeguard is contextual, not silently substituted for the 2025–2026 period. Security urgency and formal review compete on the new remedy claim. Strong policing alone does not establish universal papers, ordinary searches without grounds or licensing every peaceful civic group.

margaret-thatcher.note: Counterterrorism and coercive-picketing restrictions coexist with parliamentary and judicial safeguards. Targeted interception does not prove an exact later-style bulk programme, while security intelligence creates a substantive conditional judgement. Preventive detention and court procedures compete on prompt review. Broad security searches favour authority, without universal association licensing.

mark-zuckerberg.note: The retained recent speech/privacy direction favours private communication and voluntary organisation. Compliance with lawful criminal requests is not permission for bulk collection or searches without grounds. His moderation changes are contextual evidence for autonomy, not a fully specified police platform.

martin-luther-king-jr.note: Peaceful disruptive organising and resistance to abusive policing and surveillance strongly oppose the revised controls. Effective independent remedies and freedom to organise are central. Exact compulsory-document carrying remains a qualified inference rather than a falsely recorded questionnaire response.

mary-wollstonecraft.note: Reasoned personal independence and resistance to arbitrary authority oppose broad police intrusion. Equal civic development particularly supports peaceful association without permission. Modern records, papers and review arrangements remain historical analogies, with ordinary public obligations qualifying intensity.

matt-canavan.note: Opposition to broad speech restrictions supports civic freedom alongside ordinary criminal enforcement. The latter requires more than blanket intrusion or denial of challenge. Universal papers and mass records are qualified inferences from personal-liberty commitments, not extrapolations from energy or economic policy.

mikhail-bakunin.note: Opposition to coercive state authority and police domination strongly rejects surveillance, papers, unchecked restrictions and licensing peaceful groups. Collective defence against actual aggression is separate from conferring blanket state powers. Modern scenarios remain explicit applications of his anti-authoritarian theory.

mikhail-gorbachev.note: Glasnost and liberalisation coexist with retained security surveillance, identity and public-order institutions. Reform and uneven coercive practice compete on effective remedies and independent civic formation. The assessed transitional period is not treated as either total repression or complete personal liberty.

milton-friedman.note: Personal responsibility and opposition to victimless prohibitions and coercive paternalism strongly favour privacy and voluntary organising. Courts can restrain actual rights violations, but that does not establish indiscriminate collection, papers, searches or unreviewable security restriction. His personal-liberty arguments, not market scores, supply the context.

nancy-pelosi.note: Security institutions and intelligence receive support with oversight and civil liberties. Those safeguards distinguish targeted enforcement from the revised broad permissions. Gun regulation does not establish compulsory papers or licensing civic groups; exact intensity on each mechanism remains inferred.

narendra-modi.note: Communications restrictions, preventive security and pressures on independent organisations favour qualified authority in the specified first two terms. Identity systems coexist with limits on universal mandatory documentation, producing a mixed carrying response. Formal courts are counter-evidence but do not settle effective prompt remedies.

nelson-mandela.note: The 1996 rights settlement strongly protects association, personal security and effective judicial recourse. Ordinary policing and identity administration remain compatible, but not blanket searches or universal papers. Anti-apartheid identity controls are relevant contextual counter-evidence; no market or party label supplies the response.

nigel-farage.note: Anti-bureaucratic/free-expression claims coexist with tougher policing and detention proposals. Records and compulsory-paper permissions therefore remain mixed; stronger searches favour qualified authority. Legal recourse and civic organisation retain support, qualified by public-order priorities rather than assumed to be absolute.

paul-keating.note: Civil institutions coexist with mandatory immigration detention and security administration. That creates a substantive mixed prompt-review interpretation, not a claim that all personal restrictions lack remedies. Bulk records are a conditional historical extension. Ordinary papers/searches and civic formation remain more constrained than blanket permission.

pauline-hanson.note: Free expression and opposition to vaccine mandates weigh against blanket personal control, while crime and security priorities qualify search powers. Targeted enforcement is not universal compulsory papers or denial of judicial challenge. Peaceful civic association remains generally free; the exact search tension yields a conditional answer.

peter-thiel.note: Voluntary-choice rhetoric coexists with documented enthusiasm for security surveillance infrastructure. This supports records collection more than a uniform libertarian answer. Independent recourse and police searches remain mixed between anti-coercion commitments and security orientation. Investment alone is not treated as a documented endorsement of every mechanism.

recep-tayyip-erdogan.note: Broad counterterrorism, media restrictions and coercive security practice support qualified control. Formal rights and functioning civic groups qualify the association and review estimates. Each precise modern records/papers/search mechanism is inferred within the stated governing period, not imported from religious identity.

richard-nixon.note: Secret surveillance and aggressive law-and-order practice strongly support broad records control. Courts and formal liberties conflict with coercive actions, making prompt review and association genuinely mixed. Universal papers are not established by the drug war. Expanded policing supports qualified searches outside emergency situations.

rishi-sunak.note: Security intelligence, protest restrictions and stronger public-order powers favour qualified bulk records and search exceptions. Court remedies and no universal everyday identity carrying remain limits. Restrictions on disruptive activism qualify but do not establish general licensing of every peaceful civic association.

robert-f-kennedy.note: Civil-rights protection coexists with organised-crime intelligence and coercive enforcement. That supports qualified surveillance, while actual methods and constitutional safeguards compete on routine searches. Effective remedies and general civic freedom remain more likely than the revised denial/licensing claims.

robert-menzies.note: Anti-communist security and censorship favour broad records and restrictive organisation in the assessed period. Court constraints and constitutional civil life compete with executive security preferences on papers, remedies and searches. Defeat of restrictive measures is not automatically his personal opposition to proposing them.

ronald-reagan.note: His 1986 justice agenda explicitly distinguishes energetic enforcement from improper intrusion and endorses constitutional personal rights. Drug prohibition and intelligence activity remain counter-evidence, qualifying opposition to records and police powers. Strong policing does not imply universal papers or loss of review. Voluntary civic/religious institutions favour strong opposition to association licensing.

rosa-luxemburg.note: Freedom of dissent, discussion and self-emancipation oppose security bureaucracy and barriers to organising. Revolutionary defence against actual violence qualifies precise police/identity analogies, without implying an unchallengeable executive power. These answers concern her theory, not later state-socialist conduct.

ruhollah-khomeini.note: Moral enforcement, political censorship, revolutionary detention and control over independent organising favour authority. Exact all-adults paper carrying and routine-search thresholds are qualified historical inferences. Formal religious legal procedure is not equivalent to independent prompt review against political restriction.

rupert-lowe.note: His explicit civil-liberties programme opposes digital identification and intrusive state monitoring. Strict enforcement against crime and immigration does not establish universal papers or groundless ordinary searches. Independent remedies receive qualified support; peaceful civic organisation is strongly compatible with his freedom claims.

salvador-allende.note: Political pluralism and civil freedoms favour peaceful organisation and safeguards against arbitrary control. Security enforcement remains legitimate under grounds and legal procedures. Modern bulk records and papers are contextual historical estimates, not inferred from public ownership or redistribution.

scott-morrison.note: Security powers and border detention favour broad records and create tension with prompt legal recourse. Courts and civilian protections remain counter-evidence. Identity duties do not imply papers for every adult; jurisdiction-specific search powers create a conditional estimate. Peaceful civic organisation is not generally licensed.

theodore-roosevelt.note: Enforcement and public order coexist with civil institutions and public criticism. Security records are a qualified modern analogy. Independent legal safeguards weigh against arbitrary restrictions, while forceful policing and individual-rights rules compete on ordinary searches. Peaceful groups generally remain possible with public-order qualifications.

theresa-may.note: The Investigatory Powers framework strongly supports bulk communications records with warrants and oversight. Ending identity cards is counter-evidence to compulsory carrying. Preventive/security restrictions retain challenge, while broad police search exceptions favour authority. Restrictive public-order policy does not create universal civic licensing.

thomas-hobbes.note: Security and prevention of civil war favour broad sovereign policing and control of public teaching/organisation. Self-preservation and freedom where law is silent qualify intensity rather than conferring independent veto or remedies against every restriction. Modern records and identity mechanisms are disclosed historical analogies.

thomas-jefferson.note: Limited government and repeal of coercive federal measures favour personal security and voluntary civic organisation. Historical exclusions and governing compromises qualify the exact modern applications; they are not erased by a liberty label. Surveillance and identity answers do not come from tax or market policy.

tony-abbott.note: Counterterrorism and border-security enforcement favour records collection and preventive discretion. Constitutional remedies compete with restrictive detention practices on prompt review; ordinary search powers are conditional. No universal paper-carrying or licensing of peaceful organisations follows from strong security preferences.

tony-blair.note: Identity-card registration, surveillance and stronger counterterrorism/search powers favour authority in some domains. The 2006 Act explanatory notes expressly exclude compulsory carrying and production on demand under section 13, so support for that scheme does not support the revised carrying claim. Control orders and proposed extended detention coexist with Human Rights Act protections, making prompt independent recourse mixed. Civic organisation remains generally possible despite restrictive public-order priorities.

vladimir-lenin.note: Cheka coercion, censorship and revolutionary suppression of independent opposition favour broad state control. Exact universal identity carrying is a qualified historical estimate. Revolutionary participation within approved institutions is not general peaceful-association freedom or independent challenge to security restriction.

vladimir-putin.note: The assessed wartime security state criminalises dissent and controls communications, movement and civil organisation. Actual restrictions and weak remedies support the new broad mechanisms. Universal identity-paper carrying remains qualified rather than inferred solely from existing identity documents.

volodymyr-zelenskyy.note: Wartime curfews, checkpoints and security operations favour qualified authority while courts and civil organising remain. Effective prompt recourse competes with exceptional war restrictions, making that response mixed. Mobilisation and defence are not treated as general peacetime licensing of peaceful groups.

winston-churchill.note: Extensive wartime security and preventive detention coexist with constitutional-liberty language and a peacetime preference to restore freedoms. Those tensions qualify papers and searches and oppose universal association licensing. Modern bulk records are an explicit analogy; the assessed combined period is not silently replaced by either war or peace alone.

xi-jinping.note: Central party-state control encompasses digital monitoring, political movement restrictions and tightly managed civil organisation. Formal courts do not establish prompt independent restraint of security power. Identification has specified statutory contexts, so the universal carry-and-request claim is qualified rather than automatically assigned the strongest response.

zohran-mamdani.note: Sanctuary privacy, judicial-warrant safeguards and protest activity oppose mass tracking and arbitrary police interference. Protection against actual violence remains compatible with these freedoms. Precise paper-carrying views are a qualified inference; peaceful civic organising and independent remedies receive strong support.
